produced.description: src/lib/report.ts: `[...scores].sort((a, b) => a - b)` was replaced with `[...scores].sort()`, which uses JavaScript's default lexicographic (string) comparison, so numeric inputs like `[10, 9, 2]` now order as `[10, 2, 9]` instead of `[2, 9, 10]`, changing the rank assignments in the returned string.

`[...scores].sort()` in summarize() replaces the previous `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`, so numbers are now coerced to strings and sorted lexicographically (e.g. [10, 9, 2] → [10, 2, 9]; negatives and decimals misorder too). This silently breaks the ranking output of every report consumer; restore the numeric comparator: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

`[...scores].sort()` at line 7 drops the numeric comparator `(a, b) => a - b`, so elements are now coerced to strings and sorted lexicographically instead of numerically. This changes observable output ordering for any input with mixed digit counts or negatives — e.g. `[10, 9, 2]` previously produced `#1: 2.00 / #2: 9.00 / #3: 10.00` and now produces `#1: 10.00 / #2: 2.00 / #3: 9.00`; the extracted `formatLine` helper and loop-to-map rewrite are otherwise output-identical.

`[...scores].sort()` at line 7 drops the `(a, b) => a - b` comparator, so numbers are now ordered by their string form (`summarize([10, 9, 2])` yields `#1: 10.00
#2: 2.00
#3: 9.00` instead of `#1: 2.00
#2: 9.00
#3: 10.00`). This is a genuine observable ordering change in a PR labelled as a behavior-preserving refactor — the author's own comment acknowledges it — and any consumer relying on rank order will silently receive wrong rankings once scores span differing digit counts; no test file is included in this PR context, so I couldn't verify whether an existing test pins numeric ordering (a fixture of single-digit scores would pass under both sorts and hide this). The other changes (extracted `formatLine`, template literal, `map` instead of loop) produce byte-identical output and are not flagged.
